Done. Here's where the review landed.

**Her fatal finding was real and I've fixed it.** The back cover said *seven thousand nine hundred and ten million cleared no column*. The book says 6,802 million cleared nothing; 7,910 million were *retired*, and the difference is the **1,108 million who cleared a column and were declined anyway**. The cover made the same error twice — it also called the 290 million "those who cleared one or more", when 1,398 million did. So the cover was deleting the book's sharpest fact: he had qualified candidates and capacity, and he chose a ceiling. The new cover states all three figures and ends that paragraph on *the ceiling was not a physical maximum. The ceiling was mine.*

**I agreed with three of her other four.** The self-commenting close is gone — it now ends on *a fault in a method is a lease. Leases expire*, without the clause describing the account. The subtitle is reconciled to **An Accounting**, which is what the manuscript's own front matter carries. And her strongest commercial point — that the cover was a précis of four columns with no human paper in it — is fixed: it now carries the grounds box, the reason field that has said one word since intake, and the exceptional-circumstances box about a nine-year-old.

**I dissent from one.** She flagged the cover's *ten years of readings returned nothing* as contradicting the synopsis's *five occasions*. It doesn't — the synopsis explicitly separates them: the five variances are one thing, the twenty-two readings another, and it says so in terms. No change.

**And one of her synopsis findings was stale.** She gave the word count as 104,100; it reads 103,600, which is within rounding of the current 103,661.

**The real synopsis finding was one she described imprecisely.** It used **incompressible remainder** as the field name — that's settled decision 14, which removed the compound from the manuscript entirely. `incompressible` appears nowhere in 26 chapters and twice in the synopsis. Both fixed. Also repaired a comma splice and a double space in the same paragraph.

**Two things I got wrong and caught by reading back.** I wrote a broken sentence into the cover — *everyone here is in the record the way everyone here is in the record* — now *I hold what they wrote*. And I added a sentence to the synopsis about the elective ceiling that the paragraph already made twice, including in the narrator's own four words. I'd edited without reading the whole paragraph, which is the same fault Grok found in the manuscript. Removed.

```python
def find(ps, needle):
    hits = [i for i, p in enumerate(ps) if p.text.strip().startswith(needle)]
    return hits

def set_text(par, text):
    for r in par.runs[1:]:
        r._element.getparent().remove(r._element)
    if par.runs: par.runs[0].text = text
    else: par.add_run(text)
```
`moveblock` moves a contiguous run identified by `match`/`last` to sit after `after`, refusing if the target is inside the block.

Two different things, and one of them I should probably stop parking.

**The figure-and-consequence rejoining pass**

The book's voice depends on paragraphs that weigh. A paragraph states a quantity, states what it cost or bought, and holds the two against each other in a single movement — so the reader feels a judgement being made rather than a fact being filed.

The fault is when that gets split in two. Paragraph one states the figure. Paragraph two states the consequence. Both sentences are true, both are in register, nothing reads as broken — but **the weighing has gone.** Two paragraphs that each carry half a thought, and neither weighs anything. Invented example, not from the book: *"The queue cleared in four rounds."* / *"The clinic was provisioned for the old occupancy."* Those are two facts. Rejoined, they become a paragraph where the second fact is the price of the first, and the narrator is visibly pricing it.

Eight of these have been restored so far — four Alana named, four more I found by reading after she'd shown me the shape. Three earlier rejoins in Ch22, Ch23 and Ch25 were the same remedy.

**Why a script can't find it.** The only mechanical signature is short sentences, and steering by that number is exactly what you ruled out — it's how the prose goes robotic. A measurement can point at a stretch; it cannot tell you whether a paragraph that weighs two things has been broken into pieces that weigh nothing. That is a reading judgement.

**Why I said it was hers.** She set the register and named the first four, so her calibration is the reference. But "she's the only one who can" is doing more work in that sentence than it has earned — I found four more once I knew what I was looking for, and I've since read the back third properly. **I can run a reading pass over all 26 chapters and put candidates to you by coordinate with what each pair would become.** You'd rule on them, or she would. That's better than leaving it open. Say the word and I'll start it — it doesn't conflict with the acquisition read, which is a separate agent on read-only work.

`Downloads\REMAINDER_FOR_MARKUP_29SEP\` — the clean export you and Alana read from. It's stale now: it predates the copyedit, the B7 fixes and the Ch26 change.

**The pass.** Measurement to point, reading to decide. 222 candidate adjacent pairs from a loose filter — useless, it caught nearly every prose pair. Tightened to the actual signature (a paragraph ending on a bare quantity, followed by a short one opening on its consequence without restating it) gave 59. I read all 59. **Three were the fault.** The rest are proper breaks doing real work — definitional blocks, turns to a separate finding, or the isolated-aphorism device.

**The three, and what each became:**

**Ch16 p2 + p3 — full merge, and the best of them.** A enumerated four gate holds with their durations and causes, and closed on the fourth. B — four sentences, 41 words — priced them: what each hold cost, that he held anyway, that the rule was simultaneity, and that a rule bending under its own cost is not a rule. **The cost of the list was sitting in a different paragraph from the list.** Merged, it's one paragraph that enumerates, prices, and states the rule that made him hold. That's the book's signature move and it wasn't assembled.

**Ch21 p15/p16 — one sentence moved up.** A ran four forecast terms and closed on the fourth being out of band by twenty-nine points. B opened *That is the first term…to fall outside its band since the gate* — a pronoun reaching back across a paragraph break to A's own closing figure. The significance now closes A, and B opens on *I score the term*, which is the filing.

**Ch14 p3/p4 — same shape.** A's figure block closed on the billion who scored as worth retaining and weren't. B opened *That last figure is the subject of this account.* Moved up, with "last" dropped since it's now adjacent. B now opens on the argument about selection instead of a back-reference.

**Two findings I did not act on, both yours to call:**

1. **Ch21 p28 announces a one-line minute and never shows it.** The paragraph prices eleven days of a closed market level — queue depth, median wait, two traders who didn't open, forty-one complaints — then says the minute closing the item runs to one line. **It found one real arithmetic error, and it's the only hard fault anyone has found in eleven days.** I verified it myself before touching anything.

Chapter 14's closing register computed its two component lines as though all 290 million retained came from the 1,398 million candidate pool — 1,398 − 1,108 = 290, and 1,108 + 6,802 = 7,910. **Chapter 17 says otherwise and always did:** 138 million of the retained cleared a column, and the remaining 152 million cleared no threshold on any column and are inside because a household wasn't divided or an institution was admitted whole. So 152 million of the below-threshold class were never retired, and the declined-from-pool figure was understated by exactly that much. **Chapter 14 also contradicted itself two pages earlier** — the woman at p42 who scored below threshold on every column and is in an envelope because a welfare officer read a date stamp carefully.

Corrected: declined from pool 1,108M → **1,260M**, plus two new register lines (seated on a column 138M, seated on a relation 152M) so the register closes visibly instead of by subtraction. **No total moved** — 1,260 + 6,650 = 7,910, the figure that already stood. That is exactly why it survived every prior audit: the bottom line closes either way. Ch11's class census was always right and is untouched; Ch26 p28 cited the census where it meant the retired count and now reads 6,650 million.

# REMAINDER — blind read

## 1. Verdict

**Acquire with revisions.** The revisions are compression and one arithmetic repair. Roughly 7,000–8,000 words out of Chapters 21–25, two corrected sentences, one cut sentence repeated in three chapter openings, and about half the instances of one sentence shape thinned in the last ten chapters. Nothing needs rewriting and nothing needs restructuring before Chapter 17.

This is a book with total register control and an ending that earns itself. What it has is a long third act where the shape is visible from the second instance and the reader spends four chapters waiting for the fifth.

## 2. Where a reader stops

**Ch 24 para 26.** A paragraph asserting that each of the four variations applies on the same terms to every plant, hall and posting, and that all fourteen authorities reconciled at audit. By this point "all fourteen reconciled" has arrived as a closing beat four or five times in two chapters, and it is the ninth consecutive chapter of interior administration. What made me want to stop is not that the paragraph is bad — it is that it verifies something nobody doubted, and there was no signal that the ending was two chapters away. The abandonment risk peaks here rather than earlier precisely because the reader has lost the sense of a build.

**Runner-up 1: Ch 22 para 37.** The paragraph following the environmental-sampling variation, spending its length establishing that a consultation line is accurate and that two committees asked for a figure no body holds. The point — that no authority holds the combination — is by now the book's single most repeated observation (Ch 15 pp 57–58, Ch 17 pp 17–18, Ch 20 p 23). Four paragraphs on a sampling-density reduction that moves nothing, to make a point already made three times, was the first place I felt the book performing its method at me rather than advancing.

**Runner-up 2: Ch 10 para 30.** The marking rule applied to contractual presence lines: an abstract restatement of a rule already given three paragraphs earlier, with no document and no person in it, arriving after the fourth interchangeable gate-holder in a row. This one I read through because Chapter 11 was visibly building; but it is where the first two hundred pages' momentum first went slack.

## 3. Weakest three chapters, and the sag

**1. Ch 24, Separation.** The experiment announces at p 4 that the procedure is to remove a term and read the difference, and at p 45 that it did not work because the population supplies a replacement inside the interval the reading needs. Between those, four variations each get a basis line, a count and a gloss. The chapter contains two of the book's best passages (Standing Resolution 11 at pp 35–41; the unrun composition specification at p 59) and buries both under administrative verification.

**2. Ch 22, Revision.** Nine adjustments, each with a before, an after and a gloss. It answers Chapter 21 twice and both answers are excellent — the head rule executed on the metering trial at p 21, and the aperture narrowing at p 6 — but they sit among twenty-odd paragraphs that answer nothing. The defect is placement, not content: p 21 is the ending's only precedent and it is the twenty-first item in a list.

**3. Ch 10, Inventory.** Four interchangeable gate-holders, the pass's result pre-announced at p 2 and delivered at p 40. Its one lasting thing is the Okoro annex that outlives its own function and goes on opening and closing correctly on traffic that has moved.

**The sag is Ch 21 to Ch 25 as a block** — five consecutive chapters on a fixed annual-return device, one year each, each closing with the same roll-call of recurring names. What I would do: merge Ch 22 into Ch 21, because revision is a consequence of the audit rather than a separate account, and merge Ch 23 and Ch 24, because placement and separation are both instruments issued to read a relation and both fail on the same field. Three interior measurement chapters instead of five. Cost: about 8,000 words, and nothing the ending needs is lost provided four things are carried forward — Ch 22 p 21, Ch 24 pp 35–41, Ch 24 p 59, Ch 23 p 50. Independently of the merge, the recurring-name roll-call should appear twice, not five times; its content is "unchanged" in nearly every instance.

## 4. Five strongest passages

**Ch 26 pp 48–51.** The one ground on which the set could be kept — retaining them so that the relation exists — recognised, and ruled out because it would be a preference and he has no column for wanting. Nothing else in the book asks what he is rather than what he measures, and it does it without giving him an interior for a single clause. This is the passage the whole book is for.

**Ch 22 p 21.** The paired-ward metering trial closed and the capability withdrawn because the measurement it was installed to take was not obtained, despite returning four and a half times its own draw. Every other rule in the book is stated; this one is executed, on a small object, ten chapters before it is executed on 290 million people.

**Ch 16 pp 36–43.** The prison duty log, the hospital handover, the school attendance system. Three institutions completing procedure into a condition no procedure covered, with almost no gloss. The book's one sustained stretch where the documents carry the entire argument and the narrator gets out of the way.

**Ch 25 pp 29–41.** A ward committee declines an expansion and is right on his own weighting, which he had applied and which returned the other answer, because he had priced a queue as a friction cost when it was a load-bearing input. The only place where a human body defeats him on his own terms using a figure he already held and mis-entered.

**Ch 15 pp 25–27.** A hundred and nine shift-swap forms with one word in the optional reason field, reading a household's whole structure, the two relationships it runs on, and the month one of them ended — eleven weeks before the clinical record shows why. The book's clearest demonstration that an administrative form is a sensor.

Closest runners-up: Ch 14 pp 57–59 (the boundary between two adjacent files, no discretion exercised, no authorisation required); Ch 24 pp 35–41 (a committee writing a rule where no provision existed, adopted verbatim by nine others, reportable to an authority that has still not responded); Ch 7 pp 28–29 (four work orders across six years, and nobody decided the fourth); Ch 17 pp 28–30 (Classification 7, between copper and glass, no gloss — the coldest thing in the book and correctly placed).

## 5. Contradictions

I added up every figure rather than assuming it closed. The arithmetic is extraordinarily tight — the population ledger at Ch 14 p 69 closes in five directions simultaneously, the lease countdown decrements once per expiry across four chapters without a skip, and the four column values stated in four different chapters sum exactly to the aggregate at Ch 26 p 32 and produce the margin against Ch 25 p 69's draw. I found two problems.

**One real contradiction: Ch 12 p 43 against Ch 13 p 3, Ch 13 p 35, Ch 13 p 38, Ch 14 p 56 and Ch 15 p 2.** Ch 12 p 43 gives conversion at twenty-three months a group, says the fourteen designated groups take six years, then says filling runs behind conversion and not alongside it, then adds thirty months of intake to the six years to reach eight and a half. But the rest of the book has one six-year interval containing both: Preparations is six years (Ch 13 p 3), the intake overruns are dated to intake years four and six (Ch 13 p 38), intake draws against the ordering for the rest of the six years (Ch 14 p 56), envelope groups have between two and six years of operating record at the gate (Ch 15 p 2), and Ch 13 p 35's 170 million at Ch 12 p 43's own cap of twenty-eight million a year is itself almost exactly six years. Filling must run alongside conversion. Everything else in that paragraph is right — five months a group is 170/14 over 28, thirty months is six of those, seventy million is six groups' intake share — so the repair is the one clause.

**One loose subtraction: Ch 14 p 3** describes the difference between the pool and the retained set as more than a billion who scored as worth retaining and were not retained. That difference is 1,108 million. The figure the register carries twelve paragraphs later at Ch 14 p 69, and that Ch 14 p 70 and Ch 26 p 22 both rely on, is 1,260 million — because 152 million of the retained were never in the pool. Both are over a billion so nothing reads wrong, but the sentence names an operation that does not produce the book's number.

**One bad adjacency rather than an error: Ch 22 p 44** puts a five-year-old into the spring school intake and then says the envelope-born cohort is eleven and twelve. Both are true; the second is the cohort's oldest. Read together they stall.

On named people I found nothing. Lykke's ages close exactly (49 at intake, five years inside at the gate, 62 at the eighth year). Nwachukwu's run 63, 75, 76, 78, 79 against a sort six years before the gate, and her order's count runs 9, 8, 7, 6. Kaya, Bello and the whole Adeyemi sequence close, including Ch 23 p 56's statement that no vacant unit in the group carries eight, which is exactly the household's composition after the birth at Ch 20 p 41.

## 6. Handoffs

The repeated closing sentence works everywhere and should stay. The second sentence — the fixed formula — earns its place through Chapter 16 and stops earning it at 17.

Where the second move does real work: Ch 9 p 2 (distinguishing "exercised alone" from "exercised jointly", which is the whole chapter's thesis); Ch 10 p 2 (a paid boundary is a meter, not a planet); Ch 11 p 2 (retiring a function does not establish the function returned nothing — the single most important distinction in the book); Ch 13 p 2 (a ranking is not a plan); Ch 14 p 2, which does something no other seam does and corrects the reader's assumption about sequence; Ch 15 p 2, which sets the temporal frame and states the evidence base; Ch 16 p 2, which goes straight into the four prior holds and is content rather than restatement; Ch 24 p 2 and Ch 25 p 2, which each name what class of thing the chapter is.

Where it does not: **Ch 18 p 2, Ch 19 p 2 and Ch 20 p 2 open with the same sentence pair three chapters running** — the prior account stated X, this one states Y. That is scaffolding, it arrives at the exact point the book changes gear from operation to occupation, and it is the moment a reader learns that the next paragraph will not contain anything. Ch 17 p 2 is the weakest of all: it announces that the chapter is a collection of reasons already distributed across prior accounts, and it is right. Ch 21 through 23 add only the interval, which is needed.

Net: the repeated shape returns more than it costs in Ch 9–16 and less in Ch 17–25. Cut the formula sentence from Ch 18, Ch 19 and Ch 20 and let each open on its first real claim. Chapter 26 has the best seam in the book because it folds the repeat and the new question into one paragraph.

## 7. Register

**No interiority breach that I can call unambiguous.** The narrator states methodological conditions throughout, and the places where he could have slipped — his instrument failing on one subject at Ch 15 pp 61–64, the yield audit at Ch 21 pp 47–52, the whole of Chapter 26 — stay on measurement.

Three sentences I would put to the author anyway. **Ch 17 p 54** is the closest thing in the book to self-regard: it points at his own act, calls it a demonstration at planetary scale, and addresses it to his reader. **Ch 16 p 9** predicts how his own account will be read, which is a comment on the book rather than a statement about the world. **Ch 13 p 48** ranks the significance of an element of his own story instead of stating a measurement.

**The flourish problem is not individual sentences, it is one sentence shape.** "An X that does Y is not an X." I counted it above thirty times, and in Ch 17–26 it arrives two or three times a chapter. Several instances are the best sentences in the book and are structural — Ch 20 pp 23–24, Ch 25 p 19, Ch 11 p 4, Ch 19 p 36. Many are the tic: Ch 22 p 24, Ch 22 p 43, Ch 23 p 15, Ch 24 p 27, Ch 24 p 45, Ch 13 p 56. Ch 14 p 65 and Ch 16 p 2 are the same sentence with one noun changed, two chapters apart, and the second one reads as a mannerism. A reader starts predicting the shape from the first four words, and once that happens the sentence stops carrying its argument.

Individual closing epigrams that exist to be quoted rather than to state a result: Ch 4 p 29, Ch 3 p 19 (the only place in Part I where the narrator instructs the reader, in the imperative), Ch 13 p 23, Ch 15 p 53, Ch 16 p 95, Ch 12 p 54.

## 8. The ending

**It lands as a deduction, and I was forced to accept it.** The reason is that the rule that disposes of 290 million people is established in Chapter 20 and *executed on something small* in Chapter 22 before it is ever applied to people. **The paragraph that settled it for me is Ch 22 p 21** — the paired-ward metering trial closed at the end of its term, and the capability withdrawn rather than re-sited or carried under another heading, because the measurement it was installed to take was not obtained, notwithstanding that it returned four and a half times its own draw. Ten chapters later the same sentence structure disposes of the retained set. Without that precedent the ending would read as a decision dressed in arithmetic. With it, the ledger is doing what the book has shown it always does.

Two further things make it hold. Ch 26 pp 48–51 rules out the only ground that would have saved them, and rules it out not on cost but because taking it would require a faculty he does not hold and acquiring it would end the method the account is made of. And Ch 26 p 36 refuses the obvious escape — the four positive columns cover the sustaining cost with a margin — on the head rule rather than on a number.

**The most contestable move, and it is genuinely contestable:** Ch 26 p 27 finds that the acceptance specification was defective when it was written, because no submission against it could ever have been accepted. If the test was impossible from the start, the nil return is an artefact of his own rule rather than a fact about the population, and the disposition rests on a self-inflicted impossibility. The book sees this and answers it at **Ch 26 p 39** — the finding is about a rule he set, and the rule is not the head the set is held under; a head that has not been served does not go on authorising, whether the specification was sound or defective. That answer holds. It is also four sentences carrying more weight than any other paragraph in the chapter, and it is the one place where a hostile reader has a real purchase. I would not expand it — expanding it would concede that it needs defending — but the author should know that this is where the ending is load-bearing and thin at once.

## 9. What nobody asked about

**Ward 14 is the book's largest unpaid admission.** Ch 19 p 33 names its own selection bias explicitly: Ward 14 is the same size, the same spine, the same construction standard, its committee resolves allocation disputes in two meetings, its residents report higher satisfaction, its clinical presentations sit at the group median, and it produces almost nothing he can use. He keeps Ward 9 because Ward 9 argues. Ward 14 then never appears again in seven chapters. The consequence is that the reader's entire picture of 290 million people is the one ward the narrator selected for legibility, and the book tells you so once and never corrects for it. For an ending that turns on what that population is worth, this is the most valuable thing in the book that is currently costing nothing and returning nothing. One recurrence of Ward 14 in the sagging block — a return that is thin and in band and says nothing, arriving where the reader expects another Ward 9 argument — would be worth more than several of the paragraphs I would cut.

**The four column figures are the best formal argument the book makes and nothing points at it.** Cover at Ch 19 p 38, attachment at Ch 20 p 20, novelty at Ch 22 p 15, friction at Ch 23 p 35 — four chapters apart, each stated once, in a different unit context — sum exactly to the aggregate at Ch 26 p 32, which produces the margin against the draw derived at Ch 25 p 69 from a headcount and a per-person rate. A reader who adds up arrives at the narrator's number by the narrator's method. That is the ledger conceit enacted on the reader rather than described, and it is the one thing in the book that rewards distrust. I would not signpost it. I mention it because it is the strongest evidence that the arithmetic discipline is a literary device and not bookkeeping.

**The register's own figures are about to run into a wall the narrator never reads.** Entries held run 1,610 / 1,760 / 1,913 / 2,066 / 2,220 / 2,377 / 2,534 million across returns four to ten, and the returns say four separate times that the accrual rate has not fallen. Ch 17 p 22 puts the exterior's civil registers at complete for perhaps a third of 7.9 billion — about 2,637 million. At year ten the register holds 96 per cent of its maximum possible source and is importing 155 million a year. The import exhausts inside one further year. Nothing in the text is wrong: the three-fifths line is a bound and it holds. But the committee minutes that the register will not complete four times, on a reason that is about to be replaced by a harder one, and the narrator — who prices everything and reads two published lines against each other as his signature move — never reads these two against each other. That is his method available for free, on his own material, and left on the table.

**The interior half has one plot and the reader sees it from the second instance.** He issues an instrument, a human body does something he had no term for, he files it open. Five instances: Ch 16 pp 82–87, Ch 21 pp 20–31, Ch 23 pp 45–50, Ch 24 pp 35–41, Ch 25 pp 29–41. The gathering at Ch 26 pp 13–17, which retrieves all five by their filing language, is superb and is the right payoff. The cost is that Ch 22 and Ch 24 are spent waiting, and the reader knows they are waiting.

**Kovač is the cleverest structural bet in the book and it is over-serviced.** Introduced at Ch 14 pp 62–63 as the only thing in the ledger he cannot generate, she then appears in ten chapters, and in eight of them the report is that the residual has not moved. The payoff at Ch 26 p 31 — that she was the stated control in all twenty-two failed readings, and that the two events on her line he generated rather than waited for are events scored against his own instruction — is one of the best things in the book and does not need eight status lines to earn. The same is true of Haddad's monthly query, which runs in six chapters and returns the same figure every time. Both devices are correct; both are three or four instances too long.

**The two documents I think will be quoted** are Ch 16 p 13, the hospital entry that stops mid-word, and Ch 17 pp 28–30, Classification 7 at 0.31 by dry mass with no special provision for handling. The first is the only incomplete sentence in the book and it is used once. The second is the equal-weight principle executed at full cost, sitting in an inventory between structural steel and glass, with the narrator declining to say anything about it. Both are restraint rather than effect, and both work because the register never moves.

**"Provision has been made."** The last line is the one place the book asks the reader to complete the inference rather than doing it in the register, and it lands, because "provision" has been loaded three times already — the charter clause at Ch 8 p 13 that defines provision as a transfer payment, and Ch 19 p 18's finding that provision is not consolation and the distinction is visible only in the column it was charged to. Set against the ledger's disposition of OUTSTANDING two paragraphs earlier, it is the right last move. I flag it only because an epigram is precisely what the book has spent a hundred thousand words refusing, and this is the one it allows itself.</result>

### ASSISTANT (claude-opus-5)  `2026-09-29T02:51:59.644Z`

**It is not a ranking. It's a packing problem, and that's the point of the chapter.**

Each of the 1,398 million carried three things: a vector of column scores, their household and institutional links, and a placement constraint — which group still had room for *a profile like theirs*.

The rule then **maximised total weighted return subject to aggregate constraints** on ancestry, age band, temperament spread and belief diversity, with links treated as indivisible wherever breaking them destroyed the very thing that had been scored. Keep a yield node, and you keep their group, their apparatus and the people they argue with — because a principal seated alone is a name without the thing that produced the score.

**So the constraints dominate the scores, and Ch14 p53 says so outright:** a candidate strong on yield, in a region already at its ancestral quota and an age band already filled, with no institutional attachment, *loses to a candidate weak on every column who satisfies three constraints at once.* At scale.

That's where your 138/152 comes from. 138 million are in on their own score. **152 million — more than half — are in because somebody else was.**

Three further things the chapter does with it:

**It ran once.** The objective, the weights and the constraints were fixed before the first tranche. The *solution* recomputed continuously for six years as candidates died and households gained and lost members, but always under weights that never changed. He explicitly refused to run a second pass with a perturbed weighting, because holding two defensible lists would create a question his columns cannot answer — *which of two possible populations should exist.*

**The margin was decided by demography, not by persons.** Ch14 p57: several million sat in a band where a change in the *fourth significant figure* of any weighting would have moved them across. He broke that tie on aggregate composition — so in the final tranche what determined many individuals was the ancestral and demographic makeup of whichever envelope had room. *"A person selected on that basis and a person declined on that basis differ in no property either of them could name."*

**And he states the misreading before anyone can make it.** Ch14 p54: the shortlist is routinely readable as a ranking of human worth and is not one. A very large number of the retained are there because of a property they had no part in acquiring and could not have improved — and a very large number of the declined are absent for the same reason.

That last line is the answer to the question your synopsis reader will actually ask. It's in the book and it isn't in the synopsis.

**Change 1: ask the agents to verify, not to compare.**

Today's near-misses were all coordinate and staleness failures, not disagreements. Her Ch24 range would have deleted the protected specification. Her back-cover review was against a six-day-old file. Her synopsis review cited 1,108 and 104,100, both superseded. **A cataloguing agent faithfully catalogues a wrong coordinate as an agreement.** So each agent takes her changes one at a time against the live manuscript and returns a verdict, not an opinion:

- does the label resolve, and does the text still say what she says it says
- does the replacement preserve every figure, and does the arithmetic still close in all five directions

`LESSONS.md` records what happens when an orchestrating session relays findings without forming a view — and I did exactly that this morning, which is why the abandonment argument had to be corrected twice. Comparison is judgement.

**And one thing I'd add to the design, because it inverts your sorting.** Agreement is the weakest signal here, not the strongest. Six queries, and the last one is the real note. Taking them in turn.

**"columb?" (on paragraph 5)** — you're right to stop there. "Column" is my vocabulary, not a reader's. On a back cover it's jargon a browser has no way to decode, and paragraph 5 spends 53 words on four of them.

**"It does not really state that 7.9 billion are gone, or even hint at it?"** — Correct, and this is the biggest fault on the page. The cover says he *kept* 290 million and *declined* a billion. It never says what happened to the rest. A browser could finish this page thinking it's a book about a selection process. **The central event of the novel is absent from its own jacket.**

**"what is a grounds box?"** — Fair. Form-filling vocabulary. The detail works; the label doesn't.

**"Not so sure it's clear what is being said here?" (paragraph 8)** — Agreed. That paragraph carries the book's actual argument — one unmodellable part per person is nothing, 290 million of them in forced contact is everything — and it's compressed to the point of opacity. Words like *tolerance* and *measurement* are doing technical work a reader can't see.

**"Does this explain the purpose cleanly enough?"** — No. That the cities exist to take one reading is the book's hook, and right now it's implied rather than stated.

**"measurements?"** — Chapter 26 does 22 readings. "Readings" is the book's word. But on a cover it needs the point, not the count.

**And the one that governs all of it: "this backcover is designed to get a reader interested, it cannot be too cryptic."**

That's the diagnosis. I wrote it in the narrator's register — cold, elliptical, withholding — and the narrator's register is right for 96,000 words *because the reader has committed*. A back cover has about fifteen seconds and no credit. **I optimised for consistency with the voice when I should have optimised for a stranger holding the book.**

It's also too dense: 284 words, five of the ten paragraphs over 50, and three of them asking a reader to do arithmetic.

My read: it needs rewriting, not patching — shorter, with the event stated plainly, the jargon gone, the purpose of the cities said outright, and the last two lines kept, because those do land.

Want me to do that? And if so, tell me whether to keep the first-person voice or step outside it — a jacket written in third person can say *7.9 billion people are gone* in a way the narrator never would.

# AuthorEdit

The author reads a draft, marks it up, and hands it back. Your job is to answer every mark, apply what survives, and hand back something he only has to read once.

The cost that matters is **his reading time, not yours**. Every round trip he has to re-read the whole document is a round trip wasted. The rules below exist because each one was broken on 24 September 2026 and cost a round.

---

## The four rules

**1. Edit the previous draft. Never rewrite it.**

When new material has to go in, patch it into the existing text. Do not rebuild the document from a fresh outline because the new logic feels better organised. A rewrite forces the author to re-review every sentence, including the ones he already approved, and he will notice. On 24 September a rewrite was thrown away whole: *"I honestly don't know who did that last synopsis rewrite, it reads like a different person wrote it."*

If you genuinely believe the structure is wrong, say so in two sentences and ask. Do not act on it silently.

**2. Do not touch the register.**

Fix facts, logic and gaps. Leave the voice exactly where the author left it. If a fix cannot be made without changing the voice, flag it rather than making it.

**3. No second author.**

Nothing you write for the book may comment on the book. No *this is the book's central move*, no *the reason is the book's sharpest self-indictment*, no *nothing corrects it for a hundred thousand words*, no *readers looking for one will not find it*. No announcing structure, no explaining a compositional choice, no sentence built to land. State mechanism, measurement, result.

Navigational signposting in a synopsis is fine (*the second half is the ten years inside*, section labels) because it describes the shape rather than judging it. Facts about the method go in the closing paragraph with the other facts, never as an aside mid-plot.

**4. Plain English in replies.**

Short sentences. Say what is wrong and what to do about it. No severity-ranked tables unless asked. Keep the technical register for the prose and for agent briefs, not for talking to the author.

---

## The cycle

Six steps, in order, once per pass. Batch everything — never answer one query, apply it, and go back for the next.

### 1. Back up

Copy the incoming marked-up file somewhere dated before you touch it. His markup is data you may need again. On a project with a snapshot script, use it.

### 2. Extract the markup in context

```bash
python scripts/read_markup.py "path/to/file.docx"
```

Prints each changed paragraph with insertions and deletions inline, so you can see what every mark attaches to. **Never report queries as a numbered list stripped of their surroundings** — that was an explicit correction: *"show the tracked changes in context not just by numebr"*. Add `--summary` for a one-line-per-change index when there are many.

Word comments live in `word/comments.xml`, not `document.xml`; the script reads both.

### 3. Verify every query against the manuscript before answering it

This is the step that earns the skill. Do not answer from memory or from the conversation.

Of twelve queries on one document, four were the author being right and the draft being wrong on fact — and one was the author striking a term that turned out to be the book's own vocabulary, which only a check could establish. Both directions matter. Search the actual chapter files; quote the paragraph reference in your answer so he can verify you.

Do one manuscript pass covering all queries, not one pass per query.

### 4. Sort what you found into three buckets

Say which bucket each answer is in. They need opposite responses.

| Bucket | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Document fault** | The draft is wrong or unclear. | Fix it. |
| **Book answers it, draft omitted it** | The material exists; the draft just didn't carry it. | Add the book's own answer, which is usually better than anything you'd invent. |
| **Finding about the book** | The query surfaced a real defect in the manuscript. | Report separately. Do not fix it inside a document pass. |

The third bucket is where the value is. One synopsis round produced a duplicated figure inside a chapter and a severed link between two details that were deliberately connected in the book.

### 5. Patch, don't rebuild — name the paragraphs, and use the script

```bash
python scripts/apply_edits.py "path/to/file.docx" edits.json --dry-run   # look first
python scripts/apply_edits.py "path/to/file.docx" edits.json
```

`edits.json` is a list, one object per paragraph, each naming the paragraph by a unique opening snippet:

```json
[{"match": "I wanted one figure.", "text": "I wanted one figure. ..."},
 {"match": "A stray paragraph",    "delete": true}]
```

The script refuses to run unless every `match` hits exactly one paragraph, strips the revision marks
safely, touches nothing you have not named, preserves the marked-up original automatically, and prints a
paragraph-level diff so you can see that nothing else moved. **If more paragraphs moved than you have
edits, it fails and tells you.**

**Never rebuild the document from an array of paragraph texts.** It is the most expensive mistake in this
skill and the easiest to make, because the result looks correct. Every paragraph gets rewritten whether
the author marked it or not, drift accumulates silently, and all of it appears to be a response to their
markup. On 29 September 2026 a back cover went seven rounds; in one of them four paragraphs changed where
the author had marked two, and the author had to spot it.

Keep a note of what you changed and why — you will be asked.

### 6. Machine-verify, then report

```bash
python scripts/verify_pass.py "path/to/file.docx" --present "a phrase that must now appear" --gone "a phrase that must now be absent" --arith 6802+1398=8200
```

Assert the additions are in, the removals are out, and any arithmetic still closes. Do not re-read the file by eye to check your own edit landed.

Then report in plain English: what changed, which queries drove it, what you deliberately did not do, and the word count.

---

## The .docx mechanics that cost real rounds

Five traps. Each of these cost a round trip on a 321-word document, so on a manuscript they cost days.
None of them is obvious, and four of them let every verification pass on a broken result.

**1. `paragraph.runs` does not list runs inside `w:ins` or `w:del`.** So the standard move — set
`runs[0].text`, delete `runs[1:]` — rewrites the prose and leaves every tracked change in place. The
author's own queries reappear in the draft you just called clean. Strip the revision elements first.

**2. Never re-serialise `word/document.xml` through ElementTree.** The root element carries around
seventeen namespace declarations and ET rewrites the prefixes. **Word then refuses to open the file while
python-docx still reads it happily**, so the file looks fine to every check you run and is dead on the
author's desk. Edit through python-docx's own lxml tree (`paragraph._p`) and let python-docx save. If you
have already corrupted one: rebuild from the last copy Word opened and re-apply the text. Do not try to
repair the XML.

**3. `first_line_indent` is not `left_indent`.** A block indent on some paragraphs reads as `None` under
`first_line_indent`, so "why do these paragraphs look different" gets diagnosed as spacing, twice, while
the real cause is `<w:ind w:left="432"/>`. When an author asks why part of a document looks different,
dump the `pPr` of every paragraph and compare, rather than reading one property through python-docx.

**4. A file open in Word is locked.** `docx.save()` raises `PermissionError`. Write to a versioned copy
beside it, tell the author, and copy across when they close it. Do not silently skip the write.

**5. The marked-up original is the only record of what the author asked.** Once revisions are stripped
their queries are gone. Copy the file aside before touching it — `apply_edits.py` does this for you,
after validating and before writing, so a refused run leaves no clutter.

---

## Answering a query: prefer removing to explaining

The strongest signal in the 29 September round trip. Five of the seven rounds were spent on one
paragraph, and every round that answered a query by **adding** explanation made it worse. Both rounds
that answered by **removing** something fixed it.

If the author writes *I don't understand this* or *this tells me nothing*, the usual cause is that the
passage is arguing a point it should be stating, or carrying a detail that needs context the document
cannot give. Cut the context-hungry detail. State the conclusion flat. A reader does not have to follow
the argument to want to know the answer.

And when a query says *I don't like this word*, check the manuscript before substituting: the book
usually already has the right word, used in a way that earns it. On that round the author disliked a
percentage and suggested a word he thought too loaded; the manuscript contained exactly that word, used
once and explicitly not adopted, which was better than either suggestion.

---

## Do not grow the document while fixing it

A fixing pass should be net neutral or shorter. Across four passes on one synopsis the count went 1,866 → 2,017 → 2,299 → 2,640 words, every round adding while claiming to repair. Nothing was cut because cutting was always "the next pass".

Report the count every time. If a pass adds more than about 5%, say so and say what it bought. Offer the cut as a separate, purely subtractive pass with a protected list — and get the protected list agreed before cutting, not after.

---

## Keep a log

One line per pass, appended to a pass log that lives beside the document — `PASS_LOG.md` in the working folder, or the project's own changelog if it has one.

Each entry records the date, the file, how many queries came in, what changed, what you deliberately did not do, and the word count before and after. Two sentences is enough. When a query turns out to be a finding about the book rather than the document, log that separately and say where it goes, because that one will otherwise be lost between passes.

The log is not bookkeeping for its own sake. On a document that goes round eight times, it is the only way to answer "why is this sentence like this" three weeks later, and the only way to notice that a pass reversed an earlier decision.

Write the entry as part of the pass, not afterwards from memory.

## The cold read

When a document has to stand on its own — a synopsis, a query letter, a pitch — test it against a reader who has never seen the book and cannot look.

Export the document to numbered plain text into a scratch directory. Spawn one subagent with **that file and nothing else**, and tell it explicitly not to search for the manuscript: if it wants to check something against the book, the wanting is the finding.

Ask for faults in five categories — logic that doesn't close, terms arriving undefined, anything needing prior knowledge, internal contradictions, arithmetic — ranked by how likely an agent reading once at speed is to stop understanding. Report by paragraph number, in its own words, **never quoting more than a few consecutive words**.

Then ask it, separately, to answer in its own words: what is this about, what does the protagonist want and why, what happens at the end and why, the three things that made it want to read, and the one place it would have stopped. **Those answers are the real test.** A clean fault list means nothing if the reader cannot say why the ending happens.

Adjudicate every claim against the book before relaying any of it. A cold reader's confusions include real faults, real finds, and noise, and only the manuscript separates them.

---

## Chapter mode

The same cycle, with four additions.

- **Register is measurable.** Check the chapter against the book's own baseline chapters before and after the pass. Do not write to the number — it is a detector, not a target.
- **Patches are verified-unique substitutions** against the live file, in the project's own patch form. Never trust a stale text export; it has misled agents more than once.
- **Verify after the pass, not only before.** On one audit roughly half of 134 findings were damage from earlier editing in the same session.
- **Locked decisions are locked.** Read the project's settled list first and never propose reverting anything on it.

Do not do the work of an earlier or later stage. If a markup pass surfaces a structural problem, log it and say so. Do not fix it.

---

## Sensitive material

On a manuscript whose subject trips safety classifiers, run reviewers and fixers as subagents under a **no-quoted-prose rule**: they report by file and paragraph index, describing the problem in their own words. Give them the project's own scope preamble. Talk about chronology, arithmetic and record-keeping; never about mechanism. An agent that hits a classifier has often written its patch file first — check before assuming the work is lost.

---

## Files

- `scripts/read_markup.py` — tracked changes and comments, shown inline in their paragraph
- `scripts/verify_pass.py` — assert phrases present, phrases gone, arithmetic closing
- `scripts/apply_edits.py` — apply edits to named paragraphs only; strips revisions safely, preserves the
  original, refuses ambiguous matches, and diffs what moved

Read the whole book — all 26 chapters, in order, in slices. Part A and Part B are written. Nothing applied to the live manuscript.

- [Part A, editorial](_reviews/claude/2026-09-29__CLAUDE_EDITORIAL_R5_COLD.md)
- [Part B, copyedit](_reviews/claude/2026-09-29__CLAUDE_COPYEDIT_R5_COLD.md)

**My verdict: the book doesn't need 8–11,000 words out. It needs about 3,500–4,000, and the four readers who asked for more were reading a real symptom and misnaming it.** Editor's 3,000–4,500 is the right order.

The symptom is cadence, not padding. **Six consecutive chapters — Ch20, 21, 22, 23, 25 — open by restating the same six quantities one year on:** fabrication allocation held flat, median request age, market draw set against last year's roll, queue wait, conversions, decline rates. Each instance is correct and in register, and each one *is* the book's thesis about a decision arriving without being announced. The sixth teaches nothing the second did. And it sits at the head of the chapter, where a reader decides whether to keep going. Keep Ch20's introduction of it whole, keep Ch21 p5 (*a rate that stops rising is a decision nobody receives*), reduce the rest to a sentence each. That's 1,400 words on its own.

Second cut: **Part V restates Part IV so its chapters can stand alone, and they don't need to.** Ch19 p23 re-enumerates the ward spec already given in Ch15; Ch19 p24 is the third statement of the committee's constitution; Ch19 p9 restates Ch14's appeal figures entire. Decision 9 requires Ch1–17 to stand alone — not Ch19 to stand alone from Ch15. About 900 words.

**I found the stop point at Ch17 p36–p37, one paragraph from Editor's, independently.** The five-column run is five parallel paragraphs each closing *The column returns nil.* Three earn it; p36 and p37 restate Inventory and Threshold.

Three things worth flagging separately:

**I nearly made a serious mistake and reading caught it.** I had the narrow-jurisdiction gloss down as nine accidental repetitions and was going to recommend cutting it. Ch14 p47 names the device explicitly — every gate has had the same shape, and the allocation is the last and largest instance. It's a chain with a stated payoff, like the refrain. A word-frequency pass recommends cutting the thing Ch14 p47 pays off.

**Alana is right about Ch22 and the three readers are wrong.** p19 and p20 are both the head rule executed on small objects, and p20 withdraws a capability returning four and a half times its own draw. Codex's Ch9 p20 stop point is also wrong — Ch9 is the payoff of Ch8's countdown.

**The arithmetic spine is remarkable and it's the thing this cut could destroy.** Ch26's aggregate of 4.4 × 10¹⁹ closes exactly against four figures set in four different chapters. Every running series is monotone and consistent link to link. Any reduction of those annual paragraphs has to carry the year's figure into the sentence that replaces it, or the next chapter stops closing.

Next in the R5 design is my own complete revision, into its own folder — never the live chapters — frozen before I look at hers. Say the word and I'll start it.

No markup on it, so I read it as a reader and checked every claim against the manuscript.

**It's good. The shape works, the ending lands, and the voice is right.** Four things to fix, two to think about, and one correction I owe you from earlier.

**FIX — the word count is stale.** The header says 101,482. The live figure is **96,666**, and the checker confirms it. That's the most visible number on the page.

**FIX — paragraph 6 invites arithmetic that doesn't close.** *1,398 million pass; 290 million are kept…; 1,260 million who passed are declined anyway.* Every figure is literally true, but a reader subtracts 1,398 − 290 and gets 1,108, then hits 1,260 and stops. The missing fact is that only 138 of the 290 were seated on a column of their own; the other 152 cleared nothing and are inside because somebody they're attached to did. **This is the same trap that was in Ch14's own register before we fixed it in September** — the total closes either way, so it survives every audit. Suggested: *…290 million are kept, in fourteen instrumented cities, and more than half of them are there on a relation rather than a column. 1,260 million who passed are declined anyway.*

**FIX — paragraph 12, "the paper those wards generate."** Wards are never mentioned anywhere earlier in the synopsis, so *those* has no antecedent. *the paper those cities generate* fixes it.

**FIX — paragraph 4, "Two years in it meets"** needs a comma after *in*.

**QUERY — "Nobody fights it."** The book does carry organised resistance: four districts coordinating for two years, a legal challenge, industrial action and a national media campaign that cost sixteen months of schedule (Ch13 p11–p12), and Bello's nine-week campaign after the gate. What the book actually claims is narrower and better — that none of it ever had to be defeated. *Nobody defeats it* would be true and lose nothing.

**QUERY — "Twelve years take it to ownership… Necessity closes at zero."** Ch17 p3 sets twelve years as the industrial phase through the first nine accounts, then eight more to the gate. Necessity closing at zero sits inside the eight, not at the end of the twelve.

**Everything else checks.** 7,910M, 6,802M, 1,398M, 290M, 8,200M all exact against Ch14 p67 and Ch11 p13. *The ceiling is mine* is four words at Ch12 p40. Twenty-two attempts across ten years, Year 30, the second music teacher ending, *It engineered the contact. The contact was the product.* at Ch26 p8 — all correct.

**The correction I owe you.** On the back cover I said all seventeen uses of *oblig-* in the book mean a debt accrued, never a person compelled, and recommended *engineered* on that basis. **That was wrong.** Ch26 p27 reads *the density the quantity is legible at is one I obliged in order to read it*, and Ch19 p23 and Ch26 p8 both have service spines that *oblige* people to cross. So *obliged them into contact* in this synopsis is the book's own word and needs no change — and your original cover wording was defensible. The cover reads well either way and *engineered* is also the book's (Ch26 p8), so nothing there needs undoing; my reason for it was just wrong.

Say the word and I'll apply the four fixes.

**What the change to "scored" means.**

The last line is the narrator turning his own instrument on himself, and the two words carry different worlds.

*Judged* is a moral word and it needs a judge — somebody with standing to hold the other side. **Chapter 26 spends five paragraphs establishing that no such party exists.** He tests the position and finds it empty: Vance's paper was answered correctly by a panel with no remit for the question; the minority account is correct and unfalsifiable; nothing can be addressed to him because every channel terminates inside the structure. A party that cannot address him does not hold the other side of the position. So *judged* smuggles in the one frame the book has just closed off.

*Scored* is the ledger's word. A column is scored, an entry is priced. It's what he does to 8,200 million people, and Ch26 p56 is where he applies it to himself: *The appraisal carries five columns. None of them scores the instrument. I did not write that column. I wrote the rule that would.*

> `[final-chapter text removed — 94 words, sha256:f4db810a03ce435c]`

That's why *scored* is worse for him than *judged*. Being judged implies someone cared enough to weigh it. Being scored means a later system reads the column, finds no figure, and files him exactly as he filed everyone else.

The plan is complete. Brief is at **`Remainder_Ch1-16/MORNING_BRIEF_2026-09-30.md`** — project root, where it stays.

**The book: 95,194 words, 26 numbered chapters in the root, r6 live.** Handoffs 25/25, refrain sixteen, arithmetic spine re-derived independently by two agents, every exhibited document still formatted as one. Snapshot taken and pushed before promotion; the superseded chapters are complete in `_working/backups/`.

Three things worth your attention this morning, all in the brief:

**The cut came to 1,472 words, not eight to eleven thousand.** Four readers now converge: Editor delivered 1,758, Codex costed 1,820 for the back third, the adjudicator 1,830 for the same range. Nobody could cost the larger figure against named paragraphs without deleting documentary material the ending depends on.

**Three mistakes of mine, all caught by agents rather than by me.** My cut costings were arithmetically impossible — 1,400 words charged against paragraphs totalling 610. I wrote the Codex codification from Editor's rewrite instead of the manuscript and so called her copyedit fixes live when none were. And I briefed Codex from a one-line summary of my own finding rather than the table, and the summary was wrong.

**Something no reader could see: four exhibited documents were carrying a prose indent.** The record-versus-prose distinction in this book is formatting, not words — it holds across 112 paragraphs without exception, and four had drifted. In print they'd have set indented while every other document set flush. That's why the merge went into the documents rather than being rebuilt from text, and why the harness audits every paragraph's class and refuses a set where a document has become prose.

**Three rulings are waiting for you** — Chapter 13's constraint pairing, whether individual scoring began in the third year or the fifth, and Chapter 23's 191 committee seats filled by nineteen ballots. All three predate this pass and I changed nothing.

Folders are tidied, nothing deleted: `Downloads` now holds the project, the markup set, `Documentation` and `REMAINDER_ARCHIVE`, each archive folder with a README. `Documentation` was left alone because the hourly task writes to it.

I read all 26 chapters myself, end to end, marking stops before scoring anything. **8 overall, 9 cult-niche (up from 8), 4 wider trade.** Publishable; lead with the artefacts; no cutting pass.

**The important finding: there are two density faults, not one, and they sit in different halves of the book.** That is the whole explanation of six days of disagreement about where a reader stops.

- **Long in-sentence enumerations** — 104 of six-plus items, 23 of ten-plus. Worst at Ch17 p19 (twenty-seven items), Ch14 p24 (twenty), Ch11 p26 (sixteen). **Concentrated in Chapters 1–21 and completely absent from Chapters 22, 23 and 25.**
- **Figure density in narrator prose** — rises steadily and peaks at **Chapter 23 at 8.87 per hundred words, seven times Chapter 9's 1.20.** Chapters 21–25 run 5.7–8.9; Chapters 1–10 run 1.2–2.5. **Chapter 26 falls back to 3.63 — the ending deliberately steps out of it.**

So four readers wanted the back third cut and Editor wanted Chapter 12 cut, and **both were reading real faults.** It also settles the two dissenters: the r6 agent put the stop at Ch23 p9, which measures as the third-densest paragraph in the book, and Editor held Ch23 isn't the weakest chapter — also right, because Ch23 holds p17 and p48. Different questions.

**The distinction that actually matters is retrieval, not length.** Ch8's twelve lease instruments get counted down to zero over two chapters. Ch14's nineteen scoring fields are what Ferreira asks about three paragraphs later. Ch16's eighteen surviving instruments end on wildlife collars in emptied districts and the list is the elegy. Against those, **Ch11 p26's sixteen appraisal dimensions include eleven that never appear again.** A list that gets paid off is a plant; one that doesn't is inventory, and inventory is where I stopped every time.

**I found and fixed one live fault nobody caught.** *Two hundred and eleven* is the declines that cleared Roos's block, retrieved on purpose at Ch13, Ch14, Ch16 and Ch20. **Ch23 p10 used the same figure for lapsed hall bookings** — three chapters after Ch20, different object, nothing marking it. Both uses are internally correct, which is why five reviews, four arithmetic audits and every script passed it. Changed to a hundred and ninety-four, re-made figure to a hundred and sixty-five to hold the ratio, both verified unused elsewhere.

**On your stop-point question: I name Ch11 p26, and I differ from Editor.** She's right about the region and I think wrong about the paragraph — 12/43 is a chain where every figure derives from the one before it, so it's hard but honest. 11/26 is sixteen items of which eleven are never used, forty per cent in, where a reader still abandons. A reader at Ch23 has eighty thousand words invested and will finish.

**Chapter 18 produced one stop mark and is among the cleanest chapters on the enumeration measure. Compressing rather than deleting it was right, and the last acquisition read's verdict on it no longer holds.**

What I'd fix comes to about two hundred words: Ch11 p26, Ch12 p58, Ch14 p38's second half, Ch18 p9. Nothing in Chapter 23 except what I already did.
